principles.text: Build an audience first; distribution is the hard part, and a small audience can seed the whole product.
An MVP exists to learn. Test the riskiest assumption with existing tools before you build anything.
Community is secondary to utility. No one wants to join a community; they want something that solves a problem.
Start narrow. A tight focus makes the product, messaging and go-to-market easier; expand later.
Do unscalable personal outreach first, then productize what works.

sampleQA.question: How should I validate a startup idea before writing code?

answer.text: List your assumptions and test the riskiest one first with landing pages, Wizard of Oz tests or interviews.
Product Hunt started as an email list set up in about 20 minutes; organic signups gave enough confidence to keep going.
Unprompted praise from users was the signal to build the real site.
Charging money with Typeform plus Stripe is the ultimate demand test.

sampleQA.question: What did Ryan get wrong at Product Hunt?

answer.text: He would have monetized earlier, even with a small slice of focus before funding.
Expanding into other verticals like gaming too soon was a mistake; he should have gone deep on tech.
A fully flat org backfired, and cosmetic redesigns were a trap that didn't move metrics.

sampleQA.question: How do I launch so it actually works?

answer.text: Decide why you're launching first; customer acquisition is only one possible goal.
Use clear imagery and a clear tagline, test with people who don't know you, and speak like a human, not a marketer.
Treat launching as continuous: email list, beta, site, then each new feature.
